expected_evidence: Geological: platinum/iridium/other platinum-group-element enrichment layer in Greenland ice cores (e.g., GISP2, NGRIP) dated to ~12,900 cal BP / ~10,950 BCE — this is the specific signal (Petaev et al. 2013 platinum anomaly) that YDIH proponents cite as ejecta fallout evidence
Geological: nanodiamonds, magnetic/glassy spherules, meltglass and shocked-mineral fragments in the same ice/sediment horizon

Astronomical/geological: a source crater or airburst signature (e.g., subglacial Hiawatha crater), though its age has been independently dated to far older than 10,950 BCE by recent studies, weakening the causal link

Material/archaeological: discontinuity or decline in occupation sites (e.g., Clovis complex collapse) and megafaunal extinction records in North America/Eurasia, used as proxy for 'population-demography' impact
Genetic: population bottleneck or extinction signatures in ancient human/faunal DNA coincident with the YD onset
model-prior: the broader Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis literature and its ongoing, unresolved scientific controversy

Direct demographic evidence of a human population IN Greenland itself at 10,950 BCE is not expected to exist, since archaeological consensus places first human settlement of Greenland millennia later (~2500 BCE), which is a major structural problem for placing 'population-demography' impact at this specific location
response.rationale: Interval -10950 aligns with the Younger Dryas onset (~12,900 cal BP), so I evaluated against the 'younger-dryas' row (closely bracketed by 'upper-paleolithic'). The core physical claim — ejecta/fallout signature preserved in Greenland ice — has real precedent (a documented platinum anomaly in GISP2 ice cores at this horizon, model-prior, unverified beyond general recollection), and ice-sheet geological archives have comparatively high detectability (0.6–0.7) because ice stratigraphy preserves fine-grained chronological signals well, unlike most other Paleolithic contexts. This supports could_have_survived=true for the impact-ejecta-fallout mechanism itself. However, the hypothesis's object is 'population-demography' at place='greenland-ice-sheet' — this is a poor structural fit, since archaeological consensus (model-prior) holds that Greenland had no human population at 10,950 BCE; first settlement is generally dated millennia later. So while geological/astronomical fallout evidence is plausible and moderately detectable, direct demographic corroboration specifically located in Greenland is not something that could exist to be found — its absence should be read as a category mismatch in the hypothesis rather than a detectability failure. Genetic (0.3) and material (0.35) detectability for human-population effects are low for this period regardless, and any demographic effects would more plausibly be evidenced in North America/Eurasia archaeological/genetic records, not in the Greenland ice sheet itself. I weighted the adjustment down from the higher geological/astronomical values to reflect this place-object mismatch while still crediting the real detectability of an ice-core fallout signal.
